newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FORECAST - Israel interest rates to hold steady.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Israel interest rates to hold steady.

text.p: The Bank of Israel is not expected to change interest rates when it announces its April monetary programme on Sunday, analysts said on Thursday.
They said that while the central bank is under pressure to lower rates because of a slowing economy, the latest data on money supply were worrisome.

"The central bank won't change interest rates this month. I believe we are in a trend of declining interest rates but I think the central bank will wait till next month to cut rates," predicted financial consultant Eliezer Carmel.
The Bank of Israel cut the base rate by 0.3 percentage point last month to an annualised 13.9 percent. It has lowered the base rate by 3.1 percentage points since August 1996.
But a sharp 3.0 percent rise in M1 money supply in February following a 3.4 rise in January means the central bank must act cautiously, economists said.

Carmel said he thought the bank would be less influenced by the steep 1.2 percent growth in consumer prices last month, noting that much of the rise was due to higher fruit and vegetable prices. "If you look at the hardcore inflation figure it is not frightening," he said.

Shauli Katznelson, chief economist at Israel Discount Bank, predicted inflation in 1997 would reach 10.5 percent against the government's target of 7-10 percent. On the other hand, the economy is teetering on the brink of a recession, he said.

"The Bank of Israel is in a catch. With real interest rates at 4.5 percent, there is no room to raise them. In fact there is room for a further 0.5 point reduction. But any further cuts will depend on what happens to money supply, which is strongly linked to future inflation," Katznelson said.
The capital market's expectations for inflation in the next 12 months have been rising and are now at 10 percent.
The central bank will also be influenced by budget data, which will indicate whether the government is reining in the deficit as urged by the central bank.
The business sector has called for steep cuts in interest rates to boost economic activity. But Adam Reuter, managing director of Financial Immunities consultants, said this was not realistic.
"I think interest rates could fall by 0.5 percent in three months," Reuter said, adding that inflation was running at an annual rate of nine percent.
Carmel said a drastic rate cut would lead to huge withdrawals from savings accounts.
"I think we are at an inflationary level of 9.0 to 9.5 percent so we could get to a target (for the base rate) of 13 percent over the next six months," Carmel said.
